text:
Johnson put the matter in a sentence that has been often quoted and seldom weighed: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). He meant it as praise. Other dramatists, as he saw them, lifted their persons above the common measure. They gave them sentiments no one ever felt and language no one ever used, and so they traded the reader's belief for his astonishment. Shakespeare's people speak as the reader himself would have spoken had he stood where they stand. Their words come out of the occasion, and the occasion is one he can imagine for himself.

This holds even where the story leaves the world we know. A ghost may walk the battlements, or witches may meet upon a heath; but the men who see them talk as frightened, doubtful, or ambitious men talk. The action rises above life while the dialogue stays on its level. Horatio, faced with the Ghost, does not declaim. He asks it plainly what it is and why it has come, much as any of us would.
